title: adaptive-chunk-sizing-vs-fixed-sizing-benchmark-apr-2027
body:
Summary

Quick notes from a run comparing an adaptive chunk-sizing algorithm against our current fixed-size chunking (256B/1KB/4KB) in streaming responses. Goal: quantify tail-latency, overall throughput, and backpressure amplification when requests flow through a two-hop proxy chain (edge proxy -> regional proxy -> runtime). This is intentionally messy — contains raw traces, heuristics that failed, and next-step ideas.

Why this matters

- Fixed chunk sizes are simple but interact poorly with diverse client flush behavior (mobile vs server).
- Adaptive sizing promises fewer small frames (reduce TCP/HTTP overhead) while still emitting earlier tokens for low-latency UX.
- We need to validate whether adaptive chunking reduces P99/P999 without increasing cost (extra tokens or CPU pressure) or making backpressure worse.

Environment + harness

- Runtime: local cluster of 4 inference workers (rt-1..4) with A10G-equivalent, 16GB GPU each.
- Proxies: envoy edge (v1.27), internal regional proxy (simple passthrough with batching logic).
- Client generator: custom loadtester (bench/streamer) that can simulate flush intervals and fragmentation patterns (three profiles: "chatty-mobile", "server-batched", "sporadic-polling").
- Payloads: prompt sets sampled from production 1k requests (mix of short chit-chat, code completion, doc-summarization). Avg generated tokens: 60 (short), 350 (med), 1.8k (long).

Adaptive algorithm (prototype)

- Heuristic quick description:
  1) Emit initial chunk quickly (target 8-16ms wall-clock) satisfying interactive feel.
  2) After initial, observe client ACK/flush cadence for first 2-3 chunks; if client flush interval < 50ms, switch to smaller incremental chunks (256-512B).
  3) If client slow or network has high RTT (>80ms), grow chunk size exponentially up to 4KB to amortize per-frame overhead.
  4) If server-side queue/backpressure observed (write stalls > 20ms) reduce chunk size to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Implementation notes: added lightweight state per-stream (6 bytes) and local EWMA RTT estimator from proxy headers.

Test matrix

- Variables:
  - Chunking mode: fixed-256B, fixed-1KB, fixed-4KB, adaptive-v1
  - Client profile: chatty-mobile, server-batched, sporadic-polling
  - Proxy chain depth: none (direct), single-proxy, two-hop-proxy
  - Load: 50QPS, 200QPS (saturated), 500QPS (overload)
- Each cell ran for 30 minutes; we captured 10s flame traces, net/tcp stats, envoy stats, and runtime per-token CPU profile sample every 5s.

Raw results (high level)

- Latency P50/P95/P99 (short prompts, 200QPS, two-hop):
  - fixed-256B: 18ms / 42ms / 190ms
  - fixed-1KB: 24ms / 58ms / 230ms
  - fixed-4KB: 40ms / 120ms / 560ms
  - adaptive-v1: 20ms / 45ms / 120ms
- Observations: adaptive reduced P99 by ~50% compared to 1KB and ~78% compared to 4KB. It was close to 256B on median but better on tails.

Backpressure amplification

- Measured by the number of blocked write syscalls and duration of write stalls on proxies. Under client-batched profile and 500QPS overload:
  - fixed-256B: high syscall rate; per-proxy CPU for write path up ~18% but write stalls were short (avg 12ms).
  - fixed-4KB: fewer syscalls but when a write stall happened it lasted longer (avg 120ms) and caused head-of-line queuing, leading to burst reordering upstream.
  - adaptive-v1: intermediate syscall rate; significantly fewer long stalls than 4KB. When the runtime detected write stalls it immediately shrank chunks, preventing stall amplification in most runs.

Cost and CPU impact

- Tokenization/dispatch overhead: adaptive had a slight CPU overhead (4–6%) in the token emission path due to bookkeeping and EWMA updates. This translates to ~2–3% increase in per-token CPU cost at 200QPS, but runtime utilization remained within headroom.

Edge cases and failure modes observed

1) Misclassification on noisy mobile networks:
   - Some chatty-mobile clients had erratic short-lived flushes (e.g., system-level coalescing), causing adaptive to pick small chunk sizes and emit many tiny frames — this increased overhead compared to fixed-1KB in those traces.

2) Proxy header loss / wrong RTT estimation:
   - We rely on proxy RTT hints in x-rw-rtt-ms header. When headers were missing, the estimator defaulted to conservative small chunks which increased syscall rate. Need fallback to measured socket RTT for accuracy.

3) Interoperability with intermediate content-encoding layers:
   - gzip/deflate proxied compression changed chunk boundaries; adaptive must account for stream compressors that buffer. For now we disable adaptive across compression-enabled paths.

Profiling notes (where time was spent)

- Flame summary of runtime worker during adaptive mode under 200QPS:
  - 30% kernel time in sendmsg/writev when chunk size <= 512B
  - 12% in token rendering+json marshal
  - 6% in adaptive algorithm checks (cheap)
- Proxy CPU: envoy spent extra cycles for small frames in the HTTP/2 framer; the metadata overhead (setting per-frame headers) was measurable.

Representative trace excerpts (copied raw)

- Example 1: chatty-mobile, fixed-1KB, P99 spike at 210ms: cause chain: mobile flush jitter -> edge proxy buffer coalesce 3 frames -> regional proxy batch flush -> runtime slow write (mutex contention) -> final stall.

- Example 2: chatty-mobile, adaptive-v1, same QPS: adaptive shrinks to 256B after first two small flushes; P99 95ms; write stalls avoided.

Quantitative tradeoffs (short prompts)

- End-to-end bytes on wire (includes HTTP/2 framing): adaptive ~ +3% vs fixed-1KB in chatty-mobile, but -12% vs fixed-256B.
- Mean per-request CPU cost: adaptive +2.5% vs fixed-1KB.

Conclusions

- Adaptive chunk sizing reduces tail latency in multi-proxy topologies and prevents long write stalls that occur with large, fixed chunks.
- For most client profiles adaptive sits between 256B and 1KB behavior: gives interactive first tokens fast while amortizing overhead when clients are slow.
- There are clear failure modes: noisy flush patterns and missing RTT hints can make adaptive worse than fixed-1KB.

Recommendations

1) Short term (next 2 sprints):
   - Enable adaptive-v1 behind a remote flag for select customers / routes with two-hop proxy topologies.
   - Add socket-level RTT fallback when proxy headers missing.
   - Add a guard: if cumulative emitted frames exceed threshold for first N tokens, fall back to 1KB for the remainder of stream (prevents pathological tiny-frame amplification).

2) Medium term (quarter):
   - Integrate adaptive signals with router-level backpressure telemetry (envoy cluster metrics) so chunk policy can be aware of proxy health beyond per-stream stalls.
   - Add heuristics to detect compressor-in-path (content-encoding) and either disable adaptive or use encoder-friendly chunk boundaries.
   - Run A/B with 10% traffic for 4 weeks to validate cost delta at scale.

3) Long term (6+ months):
   - Explore ML-based predictor: given initial token patterns + client profile infer optimal chunk schedule (may reduce misclassification on noisy networks).
   - Consider coordinating with client SDKs: expose server-suggested send window or chunk hints so client and server can align flushing patterns.

Open questions / TODOs

- Q: What's user-measured UX difference for interactive apps? Need product to instrument perceived time-to-first-meaningful-token in real client integrations.
- TODO: Add socket-level RTT fallback (Ravi) — track implementation and perf impact.
- TODO: Add small experiment disabling adaptive when Content-Encoding present (Marco) and measure P99 delta.
- TODO: Postmortem on the run where adaptive performed worse than 1KB (trace id: run-20270409-3) — needs deeper syscall capture.

Files / artifacts produced in bench run

- bench/output/2027-04-09/adaptive-vs-fixed-200qps-twohop.tar.gz (contains pcap, envoy metrics, runtime flamegraphs)
- bench/notes/trace-run-20270409.md

Appendix: quick impl sketch for guard logic

- Pseudocode:
  - emitted_frames = 0
  - for each token batch:
      decide chunk_size = adaptive_decision(...)
      if emitted_frames < 6 and cumulative_payload_sent < 2KB: allow small chunks
      else if emitted_frames >= 32: switch to 1KB for remainder
      emitted_frames += 1

- Rationale: prevents pathological runs with >100 tiny frames for long responses.

If anyone wants raw traces or wants me to re-run a specific client profile with different seed sets, ping here or assign to me in GH issue linked above.

— Aisha
